headline: Supply chains strain. IPOs shine. Budgets swell.
deck: This week, supply bottlenecks threaten missile production while SpaceX's IPO boosts market sentiment.

stories.head: Missile production faces solid rocket motor shortage
stories.body: A recent CSIS report warns that the planned 2027 interceptor buys may be jeopardized by a shortage of solid rocket motors. This bottleneck reflects the consequences of industry consolidation, where fewer suppliers mean more vulnerabilities. The irony is that as missile programs ramp up, the very materials needed to support them are becoming scarce.
stories.soWhat: In a sector that thrives on tight schedules, this shortage could delay critical defense capabilities, leaving us wondering if we're aiming for the stars or just stuck in traffic.

stories.head: NASA tightens reins on lunar lander contractors
stories.body: NASA has unveiled revised plans for the Artemis lunar lander project, emphasizing the need for Blue Origin and SpaceX to accelerate their timelines. This shift comes as the agency grapples with delays and rising costs, suggesting that even the most ambitious space initiatives are not immune to the pressures of contractor performance.
stories.soWhat: If NASA is tightening the screws on its contractors, it might be a sign that the agency is running out of patience—and budgetary flexibility.

stories.head: SpaceX shares soar nearly 20% on IPO debut
stories.body: SpaceX's shares experienced a near 20% jump on their IPO debut, reflecting a strong appetite for space stocks in the market. With a valuation now flirting with $470 billion, the company is a clear frontrunner in the space sector, even as investors weigh the risks involved in such a lofty valuation.
stories.soWhat: This surge serves as a reminder that in the space industry, perception often trumps reality—especially when it comes to market valuations.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
